newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia's teachers angry at pay delays, low status.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia's teachers angry at pay delays, low status.

text.p: Raisa Yevgrafova can't remember how many letters and telegrams she has sent to President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Cheronmyrdin asking for their help.
"Nothing ever changes, they are deaf to our pleas so we have no choice but to strike," said the former headmistress.

Like tens of thousands of other teachers across the Russian Federation, Yevgrafova and her colleagues are reluctantly preparing to join a national day of action on March 27 to protest against chronic delays in the payment of wages and pensions.

The protest, backed by the communist opposition, is seen as a gauge of the social discontent welling up in Russia as the gap widens between a few haves and the many have-nots, who include much of the traditional Russian "intelligentsia" such as teachers, scientists and doctors.
The gentle, motherly Yevgrafova is no radical firebrand.

"We do not want to strike because it hurts the children whose welfare is our main concern. We do not want to stir up trouble but the situation has become intolerable," said Yevgrafova, who heads her local teachers' union.

She said many teachers in the Kolomna region, about 100 km (60 miles) east of Moscow, had not been paid since December. "And conditions are much worse in other regions like the Far East. Some have not been paid since September," Yevgrafova said.
CASH SHORTAGES SAP ONCE PROUD EDUCATION SYSTEM

Wage delays affect millions of Russians, including miners, army officers and civil servants, but the teachers' complaints carry added poignancy in a country that has traditionally taken pride in its educational and cultural achievements.
"Surely our country has no future without a decent education system," said Yevgrafova's colleague, Galina Safonova.
"It is so degrading. Our salary is so small anyway but they can't even pay us that on time," she added.
Even teachers with years of experience usually receive less than 500,000 roubles (about $85) a month. A young teacher starting out in the profession gets less than half that.
The government blames tax dodgers for the wage delays but its critics say Russia's fiscal system virtually invites evasion because taxes are excessively heavy, complicated and random.
In a recent report the Education Ministry said it would have to keep a tight grip on spending for a long while to come as Russia charts its painful course towards a market economy.

From Soviet times the ministry has inherited a vast and expensive educational infrastructure that includes 145,000 schools, nearly 600 institutions of higher education and more than 700 scientific organisations.

About 40 million people -- a staggering figure in a country of 150 million -- work or study in the educational system, ministry statistics show. There are 21 million pupils in secondary schools alone and their teachers number 1.7 million.

Not only school teachers complain of underfunding and salary delays. Russian scientists often protest against conditions in their institutes and some have been on hunger strike to draw public attention to their plight.
Many schools and institutes have resorted to renting out rooms as storage space to companies in a bid to raise cash.
GOVERNMENT BLAMES LOCAL COUNCILS FOR TEACHERS' WOES
Education Ministry spokesman Alexander Kuzyakin said the overall picture was far more mixed than the protests and complaints suggested.

"We cannot go back to communist times when teaching methods and materials and funding were uniform across the country," he said, adding that power and responsibility had now been devolved to local authorities and to individual institutions.

He said he sympathised with teachers who had to wait months to be paid but stressed that this was not the fault of the central government in Moscow but of local councils, which are responsible for the funding of schools and kindergartens.
"The federal government is responsible only for institutions of higher education and it has no debts to them," Kuzyakin said.

But acknowledging that many regions of Russia had problems raising the money to pay their teachers regularly, he said the government had agreed an emergency funding package to help clear wage arrears in education.
"Our minister talks with the teachers' representatives. Of course conditions are hard for many but Moscow does not have the answer to all their problems," he told Reuters.
His words ring hollow for the teachers of Kolomna.
"This is a rich country, there is money, but teachers live hand to mouth, wondering how they are going to buy bread and other basics," said Safonova of the local teachers' union.
TEACHERS STILL PROUD OF PROFESSION, SET MORAL EXAMPLE
Despite their financial problems the teachers clearly take great pride in their students and are keen to show visitors their drawings, paintings and handicrafts.
"American teachers who visit our school praise our children for their artistic skills," said music teacher Olga Sukhova.
Teacher exchanges have become commonplace in recent years as Russia opens up to the outside world and the school curriculum has become far more varied and creative than in communist times.

Teachers generally say they are not nostalgic for the Soviet era when everything was dictated to them from on high. They say they just want the respect -- and the material recompense -- their profession entitles them to.
Local education official Vladimir Orlov stressed the Russian teacher's traditionally strong moral role.
"In the West the family plays a key role helping to impress moral values on children but here this vital task is performed largely by the school," he said.
In post-communist classrooms traditional religious and moral teachings have replaced Marxist-Leninist ideology.
"We are not talking just about money. It is the future of our country and its heritage that are at stake," said Sufovna.
"If we cannot find the money to pay teachers on time and guarantee a dignified wage, how will we recruit the teachers of tomorrow."
